items.stem: What is the internal energy of a system?
options: the sum of a random distribution of kinetic and potential energies of its molecules
the thermal energy supplied to the system
the potential energy of the system due to its height
the total kinetic energy of the system moving as a whole
items.answer: the sum of a random distribution of kinetic and potential energies of its molecules
items.markingKey: U = ΣEk + ΣEp of the molecules (random).

items.stem: Explain why the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.
items.answer: There are no intermolecular forces, so the molecules have no potential energy; internal energy is the total random KE, which is proportional to T.
items.markingKey: no intermolecular forces so no PE [1]; KE ∝ T [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why 1 kg of steam at 100 °C has more internal energy than 1 kg of water at 100 °C.
items.answer: The mean kinetic energy is the same (same temperature), but the steam molecules are much further apart so they have much greater (less negative) potential energy; latent heat has been supplied.
items.markingKey: same KE (same T) [1]; greater PE in steam [1] [2]

items.stem: A container holds 2.0 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 250 K. Determine the internal energy of the gas.
items.markingKey: U = N × (3/2)kT = (3/2)nRT = 1.5 × 2.0 × 8.31 × 250 = 6230 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A container holds 0.25 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 320 K. The gas is heated to 370 K. Calculate the increase in internal energy and explain why the gas has no intermolecular potential energy.
items.answer: ΔU = 156 J; ideal gas has no intermolecular forces
items.markingKey: U = (3/2)nRT [1]; ΔU = 1.5nRΔT = 156 J [1]; no forces between molecules [1] [3]

items.stem: 0.50 kg of water at 100 °C in a kettle is boiled until it has all turned to steam at 100 °C. (a) Define internal energy. (b) The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Calculate the energy supplied. (c) Explain why the increase in internal energy is less than the energy supplied.
items.answer: (a) Sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules. (b) 1.13 × 10⁶ J (c) Some energy is used to do work pushing back the atmosphere as the steam expands (W = pΔV).
items.markingKey: (a) Sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules [1] (b) Q = mL (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.13 × 10⁶ J [1] [2] (c) Some energy is used to do work pushing back the atmosphere as the steam expands (W = pΔV) [1]

items.stem: The internal energy of an ideal gas consists of …
options: random kinetic energy of the molecules only
equal amounts of kinetic and potential energy
potential energy of the molecules only
items.answer: random kinetic energy of the molecules only
items.markingKey: No intermolecular forces, so no potential energy.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Water at 100 °C turns into steam at 100 °C. The internal energy … (b) State what is meant by internal energy.
items.answer: (a) increases because the potential energy of the molecules increases (b) The sum of a random distribution of kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of a system.
items.markingKey: (a) Separation increases; mean KE constant. (b) sum of random KE and PE of molecules [1]

items.stem: Explain why a moving car does not have more internal energy than a stationary car at the same temperature.
items.answer: Internal energy involves only the random motion of molecules; the ordered motion of the whole car is macroscopic kinetic energy, not internal energy.
items.markingKey: internal energy = random molecular energy [1]; bulk KE excluded [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of molecular energies, what happens to the internal energy of ice when it melts at 0 °C.
items.answer: The energy supplied breaks bonds, increasing the potential energy of the molecules; the mean kinetic energy stays constant as the temperature does not change; so internal energy increases.
items.markingKey: PE increases [1]; KE constant, internal energy increases [1] [2]

items.stem: State and explain, in terms of molecular kinetic and potential energies, how the internal energy changes for a steel ball dropped from a balcony and coming to rest on the ground, with no change in temperature.
items.answer: U essentially unchanged once it has cooled to the same temperature; the loss of gravitational PE of the whole ball is not internal energy.
items.markingKey: direction of change in U [1]; correct reference to kinetic and potential energy [1]; link to temperature (mean KE) [1] [3]

items.stem: State and explain, in terms of molecular kinetic and potential energies, how the internal energy changes for an ideal gas expanding at constant temperature.
items.answer: U unchanged: an ideal gas has no PE and its KE depends only on T, which is constant.
items.markingKey: direction of change in U [1]; correct reference to kinetic and potential energy [1]; link to temperature (mean KE) [1] [3]

items.stem: A container holds 0.25 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 250 K. What is the internal energy of the gas?
A container holds 0.10 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 320 K. Calculate the internal energy of the gas.
items.markingKey: U = N × (3/2)kT = (3/2)nRT = 1.5 × 0.10 × 8.31 × 320 = 399 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A container holds 3.0 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 320 K. Work out the internal energy of the gas.
items.markingKey: U = N × (3/2)kT = (3/2)nRT = 1.5 × 3.0 × 8.31 × 320 = 12 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A container holds 0.50 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 300 K. The gas is heated to 450 K. Calculate the increase in internal energy and explain why the gas has no intermolecular potential energy.
items.answer: ΔU = 935 J; ideal gas has no intermolecular forces
items.markingKey: U = (3/2)nRT [1]; ΔU = 1.5nRΔT = 935 J [1]; no forces between molecules [1] [3]

items.stem: A container holds 3.0 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 320 K. The gas is heated to 470 K. Calculate the increase in internal energy and explain why the gas has no intermolecular potential energy.
items.answer: ΔU = 5610 J; ideal gas has no intermolecular forces
items.markingKey: U = (3/2)nRT [1]; ΔU = 1.5nRΔT = 5610 J [1]; no forces between molecules [1] [3]

items.stem: 0.50 kg of water at 100 °C in a kettle is boiled until it has all turned to steam at 100 °C. (a) Define internal energy. (b) State and explain what happens to the mean kinetic energy of the molecules during boiling. (c) The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Calculate the energy supplied.
items.answer: (a) Sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules. (b) Unchanged: the temperature is constant. (c) 1.13 × 10⁶ J
items.markingKey: (a) Sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules [1] (b) Unchanged: the temperature is constant [1] (c) Q = mL (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.13 × 10⁶ J [1] [2]

items.stem: 0.20 kg of water at 100 °C in a kettle is boiled until it has all turned to steam at 100 °C. (a) State and explain what happens to the mean kinetic energy of the molecules during boiling. (b) Explain what happens to the potential energy of the molecules. (c) The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Calculate the energy supplied. (d) Explain why the increase in internal energy is less than the energy supplied.
items.answer: (a) Unchanged: the temperature is constant. (b) It increases: the molecules are separated against the intermolecular attractions. (c) 4.52 × 10⁵ J (d) Some energy is used to do work pushing back the atmosphere as the steam expands (W = pΔV).
items.markingKey: (a) Unchanged: the temperature is constant [1] (b) increases [1]; molecules separated / bonds broken [1] [2] (c) Q = mL (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.52 × 10⁵ J [1] [2] (d) Some energy is used to do work pushing back the atmosphere as the steam expands (W = pΔV) [1]

items.stem: In the first law of thermodynamics ΔU = q + W, what does W represent?
options: the work done by the system
the work done on the system
items.answer: the work done on the system
items.markingKey: W is work done ON the system (positive when the gas is compressed).

items.stem: Explain why the temperature of a gas rises when it is compressed rapidly in a bicycle pump.
items.answer: Work is done on the gas (W positive) and, because the compression is rapid, there is little time for thermal energy to escape (q ≈ 0); so ΔU > 0 and the temperature rises.
items.markingKey: work done on gas [1]; q ≈ 0 so ΔU positive, T rises [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a gas cools when it expands rapidly, as when gas escapes from an aerosol can.
items.answer: The gas does work on the surroundings as it expands (W negative) with little time for heat to enter (q ≈ 0), so ΔU < 0 and the temperature falls.
items.markingKey: gas does work, W negative [1]; q ≈ 0 so U and T fall [1] [2]

items.stem: A gas in a cylinder is supplied with 400 J of thermal energy. It expands at a constant pressure of 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa, increasing in volume by 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³. Work out the work done on the gas.
items.markingKey: W = −pΔV = −1.50 × 10⁵ × (+2.00 × 10⁻³) = −300 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A gas in a cylinder is compressed at a constant pressure of 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa, its volume decreasing by 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³. During the compression it loses 750 J of thermal energy to the surroundings. Calculate the work done on the gas and the change in its internal energy.

A gas in a cylinder is compressed at a constant pressure of 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa, its volume decreasing by 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³. During the compression it loses 300 J of thermal energy to the surroundings. (a) Calculate the work done on the gas. (b) Calculate the change in internal energy. (c) State and explain whether the temperature of the gas rises or falls.
items.answer: (a) 150 J (b) −150 J (c) falls: internal energy of an ideal gas is proportional to T
items.markingKey: (a) W = −pΔV [1]; 150 J [1] (b) ΔU = q + W with signs [1]; −150 J [1] (c) falls with reason [1] [5]

items.stem: An ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston is heated. It expands at a constant pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa from 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3.00 × 10⁻³ m³ while absorbing 1000 J of thermal energy. (a) State the first law of thermodynamics. (b) Calculate the work done on the gas. (c) Explain why the temperature rises even though the gas does work.
items.answer: (a) Increase in internal energy = thermal energy supplied to the system + work done on the system. (b) −200 J (c) The thermal energy supplied is greater than the work done by the gas, so internal energy (∝ T) increases.
items.markingKey: (a) Increase in internal energy = thermal energy supplied to the system + work done on the system [1] (b) W = −pΔV (method/substitution) [1]; answer −200 J with unit [1] [2] (c) The thermal energy supplied is greater than the work done by the gas, so internal energy (∝ T) increases [1]

items.stem: An ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston is heated. It expands at a constant pressure of 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ to 6.00 × 10⁻³ m³ while absorbing 1500 J of thermal energy. (a) State the first law of thermodynamics. (b) Calculate the work done on the gas. (c) The initial temperature is 300 K. Calculate the final temperature.
items.answer: (a) Increase in internal energy = thermal energy supplied to the system + work done on the system. (b) −800 J (c) 900 K
items.markingKey: (a) Increase in internal energy = thermal energy supplied to the system + work done on the system [1] (b) W = −pΔV (method/substitution) [1]; answer −800 J with unit [1] [2] (c) V ∝ T at constant p (method/substitution) [1]; answer 900 K with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A gas absorbs 500 J of thermal energy and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?

Answer both parts. (a) A gas is compressed by doing 400 J of work on it, and it loses 150 J of thermal energy. What is ΔU? (b) A gas absorbs 500 J of thermal energy and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
Explain the sign of each term in ΔU = q + W when a gas is heated and expands.
items.answer: q is positive (energy supplied by heating); W is negative because the gas does work on its surroundings as it expands; ΔU is positive if q exceeds the work done.
items.markingKey: q positive [1]; W negative as gas does work [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why W = −pΔV for a gas expanding at constant pressure.
items.answer: The work done by the gas is force × distance = pA × Δx = pΔV; the work done on the gas is the negative of this.
items.markingKey: work by gas = pΔV [1]; work on gas negative [1] [2]

items.stem: For an ideal gas undergoing the process "gas cooled at constant volume", state whether each of q, W and ΔU in ΔU = q + W is positive, negative or zero, and explain your answers.
items.answer: q negative, W zero, ΔU negative.
items.markingKey: q negative with reason [1]; W zero with reason [1] [2]

items.stem: For an ideal gas undergoing the process "gas compressed rapidly with no heat exchange", state whether each of q, W and ΔU in ΔU = q + W is positive, negative or zero, and explain your answers.
items.answer: q zero, W positive, ΔU positive.
items.markingKey: q zero with reason [1]; W positive with reason [1]; ΔU positive (linked to temperature change) [1] [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a gas cools when it expands rapidly, as when gas escapes from an aerosol can. (b) Explain the sign of each term in ΔU = q + W when a gas is heated and expands.
items.answer: (a) The gas does work on the surroundings as it expands (W negative) with little time for heat to enter (q ≈ 0), so ΔU < 0 and the temperature falls. (b) q is positive (energy supplied by heating); W is negative because the gas does work on its surroundings as it expands; ΔU is positive if q exceeds the work done.
items.markingKey: (a) gas does work, W negative [1]; q ≈ 0 so U and T fall [1] [2] (b) q positive [1]; W negative as gas does work [1] [2]

items.stem: For an ideal gas undergoing the process "gas compressed slowly at constant temperature", state whether each of q, W and ΔU in ΔU = q + W is positive, negative or zero, and explain your answers.
items.answer: q negative, W positive, ΔU zero.
items.markingKey: q negative with reason [1]; W positive with reason [1]; ΔU zero (linked to temperature change) [1] [3]

items.stem: A gas in a cylinder is supplied with 1200 J of thermal energy. It expands at a constant pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa, increasing in volume by 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Calculate the work done on the gas.

items.stem: An ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston is heated. items.markingKey: (a) ΔU = q + W (method/substitution) [1]; answer 600 J with unit [1] [2] (b) V ∝ T at constant p (method/substitution) [1]; answer 900 K with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: An ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston is heated. items.stem: An ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston is heated. items.stem: An ideal gas expands at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
items.answer: ΔU = 0 and q = −W
items.markingKey: U depends only on T for an ideal gas.

items.stem: A gas is heated at constant volume. Which term in ΔU = q + W is zero?
items.answer: W
items.markingKey: No volume change, so no work done.

items.stem: Explain why, when an ideal gas expands at constant temperature, all the thermal energy supplied is used to do work.
items.answer: The internal energy depends only on temperature, so ΔU = 0; from ΔU = q + W, q = −W: the heat supplied equals the work done by the gas.
items.markingKey: ΔU = 0 at constant T [1]; q = −W [1] [2]

items.stem: 10 g of water at 100 °C is boiled in a boiler test rig in Hanoi at atmospheric pressure (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa) to form steam at 100 °C. The density of the water is 1000 kg m⁻³ and of the steam 0.60 kg m⁻³. (specific latent heat of vaporisation 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) Determine the thermal energy supplied.
items.markingKey: q = mL = 0.010 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 22 600 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: 2.0 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 450 K. (a) Calculate the increase in internal energy. (b) Explain why less thermal energy is needed for the same temperature rise at constant volume.
items.answer: (a) 3740 J (b) No work is done, so q = ΔU only.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3740 J with unit [1] [2] (b) No work is done, so q = ΔU only [1]

items.stem: On a p–V diagram, the work done by a gas in a complete cycle is equal to …
options: the area under the top curve only
the area enclosed by the loop
items.answer: the area enclosed by the loop
items.markingKey: Net work = enclosed area.

items.stem: Explain why the increase in internal energy when water boils is less than mL.
items.answer: When water becomes steam its volume increases greatly, so work pΔV is done against the atmosphere; ΔU = mL − pΔV.
items.markingKey: large volume increase [1]; work done against atmosphere reduces ΔU [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the net work done by a gas in a cycle can be found from a p–V diagram.
items.answer: Work done by the gas = area under the curve when expanding; work done on it = area under the compression curve; the net work is the difference, i.e. the area enclosed by the loop.
items.markingKey: area under curve = work [1]; net = enclosed area [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why heat must be supplied to a gas when it expands at constant pressure.
items.answer: At constant pressure V ∝ T, so T and hence U increase; the gas also does work. Both require energy, which must be supplied as heat: q = ΔU + pΔV.
items.markingKey: temperature rises so U increases [1]; gas does work, so q = ΔU + pΔV > 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: A gas is taken round a rectangular cycle on a p–V diagram: A (1.00 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³) → B (2.00 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³) → C (2.00 × 10⁵ Pa, 6.00 × 10⁻³ m³) → D (1.00 × 10⁵ Pa, 6.00 × 10⁻³ m³) → A. Calculate the work done by the gas from B to C, the work done on the gas from D to A, and the net work done by the gas in one cycle.
items.answer: W_BC = 800 J; W_DA (on gas) = 400 J; net = 400 J
items.markingKey: W_BC = pΔV = 800 J [1]; W_DA = 400 J [1]; net = area of loop = 400 J [1] [3]

items.stem: 10 g of water at 100 °C is boiled in a boiler test rig in Lima at atmospheric pressure (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa) to form steam at 100 °C. The density of the water is 1000 kg m⁻³ and of the steam 0.598 kg m⁻³. (specific latent heat of vaporisation 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) Calculate the work done by the water as it expands into steam.

0.50 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K. (a) Use the first law to calculate the thermal energy supplied. (b) Explain why less thermal energy is needed for the same temperature rise at constant volume.
items.answer: (a) 1040 J (b) No work is done, so q = ΔU only.
items.markingKey: (a) q = ΔU − W (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1040 J with unit [1] [2] (b) No work is done, so q = ΔU only [1]

items.stem: 0.50 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K. (a) Calculate the change in volume of the gas. (b) Use the first law to calculate the thermal energy supplied. (c) Explain why less thermal energy is needed for the same temperature rise at constant volume.

items.stem: A gas is compressed by doing 400 J of work on it, and it loses 150 J of thermal energy. What is ΔU?
Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the temperature of a gas rises when it is compressed rapidly in a bicycle pump. (b) Explain the sign of each term in ΔU = q + W when a gas is heated and expands.
items.answer: (a) Work is done on the gas (W positive) and, because the compression is rapid, there is little time for thermal energy to escape (q ≈ 0); so ΔU > 0 and the temperature rises. (b) q is positive (energy supplied by heating); W is negative because the gas does work on its surroundings as it expands; ΔU is positive if q exceeds the work done.
items.markingKey: (a) work done on gas [1]; q ≈ 0 so ΔU positive, T rises [1] [2] (b) q positive [1]; W negative as gas does work [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a gas cools when it expands rapidly, as when gas escapes from an aerosol can. (b) Explain why W = −pΔV for a gas expanding at constant pressure.
items.answer: (a) The gas does work on the surroundings as it expands (W negative) with little time for heat to enter (q ≈ 0), so ΔU < 0 and the temperature falls. (b) The work done by the gas is force × distance = pA × Δx = pΔV; the work done on the gas is the negative of this.
items.markingKey: (a) gas does work, W negative [1]; q ≈ 0 so U and T fall [1] [2] (b) work by gas = pΔV [1]; work on gas negative [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain, in terms of molecular energies, what happens to the internal energy of ice when it melts at 0 °C. (b) Explain why 1 kg of steam at 100 °C has more internal energy than 1 kg of water at 100 °C.
items.answer: (a) The energy supplied breaks bonds, increasing the potential energy of the molecules; the mean kinetic energy stays constant as the temperature does not change; so internal energy increases. (b) The mean kinetic energy is the same (same temperature), but the steam molecules are much further apart so they have much greater (less negative) potential energy; latent heat has been supplied.
items.markingKey: (a) PE increases [1]; KE constant, internal energy increases [1] [2] (b) same KE (same T) [1]; greater PE in steam [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why 1 kg of steam at 100 °C has more internal energy than 1 kg of water at 100 °C. (b) Explain why the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.
items.answer: (a) The mean kinetic energy is the same (same temperature), but the steam molecules are much further apart so they have much greater (less negative) potential energy; latent heat has been supplied. (b) There are no intermolecular forces, so the molecules have no potential energy; internal energy is the total random KE, which is proportional to T.
items.markingKey: (a) same KE (same T) [1]; greater PE in steam [1] [2] (b) no intermolecular forces so no PE [1]; KE ∝ T [1] [2]
